title: Man Utd confirm transfer target for remainder of window after Carlos Baleba twist
author: Tashan Deniran-Alleyne
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) There are even suggestions that a medical for Baleba has already been planned with the midfielder waiting for the green light to travel to Manchester after agreeing personal terms. With the Red Devils are expected to get a deal - worth around £65million - for the Cameroon international over the line, Carrick has revealed United will remain active in the window all the way up until transfer Deadline Day. Lewis Hall said to be Carrick’s first-choice target. However, a deal for the defender looks unlikely with Newcastle digging their heels in after already losing Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes this summer. Speaking in United’s pre-Hull press conference on Thursday, Carrick was asked about the club’s transfer plans, specifically around signing a left-back. He said: “I just think we're looking to strengthen the squad. We're certainly working towards that, making the most of the situation that we have and trying to improve things and trying to move forward. “You know, I said the same thing to you last time. So, yeah, certainly trying to make the most of the opportunities to finish the window stronger than we went into it. “And I think we're a good way to doing that, so far.” ![

](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/19/9/37/BalebaManUtd19082026.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960) Racing Santander defender Jorge Salinas has been touted as a potential alternative to Hall, with Man Utd scouts said to have been impressed by his performances during the Under-19 European Championships. The versatile defender has three years to run on his contract at Racing and has also attracted interest from Barcelona. Read More Interest in the 19-year-old has prompted Racing sporting director Chema Aragon to make it clear that Salinas can leave - but only on the condition that the €16million (£13.7m) release clause in his contract is triggered.
summary: Manchester United are closing in on a £65million deal for midfielder Carlos Baleba and plan to remain active until transfer deadline day. While Lewis Hall is a primary target for the left-back position, a deal is unlikely due to Newcastle's resistance. Consequently, Racing Santander's Jorge Salinas has emerged as a potential alternative, though he is subject to a €16million release clause.
key_points: Manchester United are expected to complete a £65million transfer for midfielder Carlos Baleba.
Manager Carrick confirmed the club will remain active in the transfer market until deadline day.
A move for primary left-back target Lewis Hall is unlikely because Newcastle are blocking the deal.
Racing Santander defender Jorge Salinas has been identified as an alternative target with a €16million release clause.

title: Closer to retiring than changing teams - why Max Verstappen stayed at Red Bull
author: Andrew Benson
content:
![Max Verstappen holds a microphone during the drivers' news conference at Zandvoort](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/6260/live/4ea17b40-9c92-11f1-bd28-a9dd56c45ed7.jpg)
Four-time title winner Max Verstappen is sixth in this year's drivers' championship
- Published
The news conference that followed the announcement of Max Verstappen extending his contract at Red Bull until the end of 2030 was approaching its final moments when a light-hearted remark got to the crux of his decision.
"I was closer to retiring than changing teams," Verstappen said.
The four-time champion has been facing existential questions this year about his future in Formula 1.
The first was triggered by the new engine regulations introduced this year - did he even want to continue racing in this form of motorsport?
The second followed on - if so, did he want to stay at the team that has been his home since the start of his journey at the top level of the sport?
The announcement that Verstappen had added two further years to a contract that already lasted until the end of 2028 has put both questions to bed, to a degree. But the first more than the second.
Three races into this season, after the Japanese Grand Prix, the frustrations of driving the new hybrid engines of this year boiled over in Verstappen.
The need to constantly recover energy to power the batteries, the impossibility of doing so to the extent that they are fully charged at all times, and the artificiality that had been introduced into the racing as a consequence, were too much for the Dutchman after a race at Suzuka, arguably the greatest circuit on the calendar.
"Is it worth it?" Verstappen pondered out loud. "Or do I enjoy being more at home with my family? Seeing my friends more when you're not enjoying your sport?"
By 2028, the split between internal combustion and electrical power will be 60:40 in favour of the internal combustion engine, when it is more like 53:47 now.
That will reduce - but not eliminate - the energy starvation suffered by the engines, and as a consequence make driving the cars feel more enjoyable.
Verstappen is the purist's purist. He wants to drive on the limit all the time.
So it was total anathema to him having the engines run out of battery power, robbing them of 470bhp, before the end of long straights, needing to recover energy through the fastest corners, and having power off-sets between one car and another decide overtakes.
In May, he had an experience that underlined to him what F1 had lost, to his mind.
He raced a Red Bull-branded Mercedes AMG GT at the Nurburgring 24 Hours, and he was nothing less than sensational, particularly in a first stint that took the car he shared with two other drivers from 10th to first. Only a late driveshaft failure robbed him of victory.
This, to him, was what racing was all about.
Since Japan, the complaints of the drivers - Verstappen was far from the only driver to express his discontent - have been heard by the sport's bosses.
Tweaks to the rules are being introduced over the next two years, to increase the proportion of the total power output of the engine coming from the internal combustion side.
At the last couple of races before the summer break, which is brought to an end by this weekend's Dutch Grand Prix, a softening of Verstappen's tone in F1 was discernible. And on Thursday he confirmed it.
"After the first few races, I said to Laurent [Mekies, the Red Bull team principal], 'Don't come to me with any kind of questions about the future'. Because I didn't even know if I wanted to stay," Verstappen said.
"I love racing. I had a lot of very good discussions with F1, but also with the FIA. And I think we are slowly working towards something that becomes better and better.
"Also from my side, of course, I adapted. I accept the situation that we're all in and just trying to make the best of that.
"Also with the year that I signed to, it again opens up the door maybe, you know, when potentially the V8s come in to look at that again as well."
That is a reference to ongoing discussions about the next engine regulations, due to come in by 2031 at the latest.
It says something about the mess the sport has got itself into with the latest engine rules that discussions about the next ones, due in five years' time, started even before the first race of the new power-units.
The FIA, the sport's governing body, was primarily responsible for the issues with energy starvation that have caused so much angst this season.
They were warned by teams and drivers for the last two years or more that this energy starvation situation would become an issue. But they did not listen, instead focusing on adding ever-more complexities to the rules to try to address some of the consequences of it.
![Max Verstappen holds up the second-placed trophy at the Hungarian Grand Prix this season](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/0ed9/live/05b29030-9c93-11f1-a38b-8bb91d2ef80e.jpg)
Verstappen finished second at the Hungarian Grand Prix before the summer break
Now, though, FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem is pushing new rules that would effectively turn back the clock in F1 by a decade and a half - he wants naturally aspirated V8s, ideally with no hybrid at all, or just with some electrical window dressing.
This approach misses the point somewhat, as it is not hybrid that is the issue, but the relationship between recovery, battery capacity and deployment.
It also introduces other problems, such as what would be a significant increase in the amount of fuel cars needed to start the race because the engines would be far less efficient.
On top of that, far from all the engine manufacturers are happy about Ben Sulayem's proposal.
The V8 side of it no one has a problem with. But Audi and Mercedes, for example, would prefer the engines to be turbocharged. And there is a desire in some quarters for the hybrid part of the engine to be more significant than token.
But none of that should be a concern for Verstappen. The key point is that his main concern - being able to use all the power the engine has whenever he wants it - should no longer be an issue, with whatever new rules are produced, and whenever they come in.
And that is how Verstappen has come to make peace with where things are at.
"Personally, I'm not happy with it," he said. "It's, let's say, not fantastic. But I still love racing. I mean, it's still a Formula 1 car."
That decided, it brought him to the secondary part - stay at Red Bull, or consider a move?
Mercedes have been long-time suitors, and although they had indicated they were likely to stick with Kimi Antonelli and George Russell for next year, the temptation to make room for Verstappen had he pushed for a move would have been tough for boss Toto Wolff to resist.
Verstappen also had talks with McLaren, where his friend and long-time race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase is moving in the future by 2028 at the latest.
![Photographs take picture of Max Verstappen's car as he competes in the 24h Race at Nurburgring in may](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1024/cpsprodpb/33fb/live/d9b55020-9c93-11f1-a38b-8bb91d2ef80e.jpg)
Verstappen's involvement in this year's Nurburgring 24 Hours created a lot of interest in the race, with weekend tickets selling out for the first time in the event's history and organisers saying a record 352,000 attended
Red Bull have had a difficult 2026 so far - Verstappen is yet to win a race, and has repeatedly voiced his frustrations about the car's performance.
Mekies would not elaborate on what he called the "strategic decisions" he has shared with Verstappen, but clearly they were enough. The fact that Red Bull allow him to pursue his extra-curricular actives, such as the Nurburgring 24 Hours, without pushing back was also a factor.
"First of all, you need to feel good where you're at," he said. "Red Bull allows me to do things also a little bit outside of Formula 1. So it's, like, a big plus. You know, all of it, the whole package, which I'm very grateful for."
He talked about his love for Red Bull, about what he called a "really, really good, very open and transparent" relationship with Mekies.
Verstappen and Mekies would not elaborate in public on the details of the new contract they have negotiated.
But the deal, according to insiders, involves a small pay bump to what was already the biggest driver salary in F1, and leaves Verstappen still in control of his own future, with options to leave if expected performance is not delivered.
But it also, as Mekies pointed out, amounts to "a demonstration of trust Max has put in the team".
Verstappen said: "I always said - and I said this when Dietrich [Mateschitz, the late Red Bull co-owner] was still alive - my goal and target is to finish my career in this team. We are getting close to that.
"Of course, there's still a lot of years ahead, but that's still the target."
summary: Four-time Formula 1 champion Max Verstappen has extended his contract with Red Bull until the end of 2030, noting that he was closer to retiring than changing teams amid frustrations with current engine regulations. Concerns over the artificiality and energy starvation of this year's hybrid power units initially made him question his future in the sport. However, rule tweaks, ongoing discussions about future engine regulations, and Red Bull's flexibility regarding his outside racing interests ultimately persuaded him to stay and target finishing his career with the team.
key_points: Max Verstappen extended his Red Bull contract until the end of 2030, stating he was closer to retiring than moving to another team.
The driver faced existential doubts about F1 early in the season due to frustrations with the new hybrid engine regulations and energy starvation.
Discussions with F1 and the FIA regarding rule tweaks and future engine regulations helped soften Verstappen's stance.
Red Bull permits Verstappen to pursue outside racing activities, such as the Nurburgring 24 Hours, which played a key role in his decision to stay.

title: Liverpool see £50m bid for Yankuba Minteh rejected by Brighton
author: Andy Hunter
content:
Liverpool have had a £50m bid for Yankuba Minteh rejected by Brighton. The club are looking to add two wide forwards to Andoni Iraola’s squad before the transfer deadline, with their pursuit of Paris Saint-Germain’s Bradley Barcola continuing.
Liverpool’s shortlist of targets also includes Minteh but Brighton, who have lost Danny Welbeck to Chelsea and have Kaoru Mitoma out injured, have rebuffed the approach for the 22-year-old winger.
Minteh has scored nine goals in 66 Premier League appearances since joining Brighton from Newcastle for £30m two years ago and is reportedly open to becoming a Liverpool player. He is recovering from surgery having suffered a leg injury in a pre-season friendly against Roma this month and could be sidelined for another eight weeks. It remains to be seen whether Liverpool increase their offer for the Gambia international.
Liverpool have added the versatile Victor Muñoz to their forward options this summer for £34.5m but are yet to fill the right-sided void created by Mohamed Salah’s departure. Minteh has mostly operated on the right for Fabian Hürzeler’s team.
PSG’s £145m valuation of Barcola has forced Liverpool to consider alternative wide options including the France international’s teammate Ibrahim Mbaye. Interest in Mbaye has not developed into an offer for the 18-year-old at this stage, however.
Curtis Jones has been given permission to undergo a medical in Italy after Liverpool agreed a £30m deal with Inter for the midfielder. The Italian champions made a breakthrough in their long-running pursuit of the 25-year-old when offering €30m plus €5m in bonuses on Wednesday.
summary: Liverpool have had a £50m bid for Brighton winger Yankuba Minteh rejected as they seek to strengthen their attacking options before the transfer deadline. The club is also pursuing other wide forwards, including PSG's Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye, while dealing with the right-sided void left by Mohamed Salah's departure. Meanwhile, midfielder Curtis Jones has been granted permission for a medical in Italy following a £30m agreement with Inter.
key_points: Brighton rejected Liverpool's £50m bid for 22-year-old winger Yankuba Minteh.
Minteh is currently recovering from leg surgery and could be sidelined for another eight weeks.
Liverpool are exploring alternatives like PSG's Bradley Barcola and Ibrahim Mbaye due to valuation issues.
Curtis Jones is set for a medical in Italy after Liverpool agreed a £30m deal with Inter.

title: Why Carlos Baleba could be the missing piece in Manchester United’s new midfield
author: Lawrence Ostlere
content:
There is inherent risk with any major transfer, and perhaps the biggest gamble Manchester United are taking, should they sign Brighton’s Carlos Baleba, is that they don’t yet quite know who he is or what he might become.
Is he the brilliant teenager who commanded Premier League midfields when he first arrived at Brighton, or the 22-year-old of last season who let that form slip away? Is he a defensive midfielder who stitches play together, or a box-to-box all-action superhero? Is he a destroyer of oppositions’ plans, or something altogether more refined?
Baleba grew up in Cameroon where his footballer father put him on a gruelling training programme aged 10, and he was signed by Lille on his 18th birthday. His performances in France pinged radars at Jamestown Analytics, the secretive company informing Brighton’s recruitment, and Baleba moved to the Premier League in a £23m transfer.
I was at the Amex for Baleba’s first Premier League start and he was thrilling to watch, the best player on the pitch in a frantic 2-2 draw with Liverpool. He used his athleticism to snuff out fires all over the field, but he also had the technical skill and unbridled confidence to sashay through Liverpool’s midfield with the ball at his feet. It was all the more remarkable given his mother had died just a few months before he left France.
His then manager, Roberto De Zerbi, thanked Brighton’s recruitment department for finding another gem. “He’s very young, a very good player with incredible potential,” De Zerbi said, “and he can be one of the most important midfielders in Europe in the future.”
His very next game was a 2-1 defeat by Manchester City, and a chastening experience – Baleba later admitted he couldn’t keep up with the pace of the game. He worked hard to adjust to the Premier League’s rhythms over the following months, and gradually established himself as an important cog in Brighton’s machine.
His qualities came to the fore in an outstanding second season that sparked United’s interest. Baleba ranked highly among Premier League players for ball recoveries and interceptions, and was able to cover huge ground to break up attacks and stop dangerous transitions.
But Baleba proved to be much more than just a defensive midfielder. His ability on the ball, honed playing as a winger in youth football, helped him evade the press, wriggling his way out of cul-de-sacs and driving upfield. He headed the ball like a man four inches taller than his 5ft 10in frame, dribbled like a forward player, and racked up progressive carries to match the best in Europe.
United were ready to pay up to £70m for Baleba last summer, but Brighton wanted more than £100m, pitching his price in line with his predecessor, Moises Caicedo, who Chelsea bought for £115m. The clubs were too far apart and a deal never materialised.
The speculation appeared to affect Baleba in last season’s Premier League campaign. So did a niggling injury which he played through, as well as a calendar broken up by the Africa Cup of Nations, and he completed only three full 90 minutes in the league. The nadir came against Aston Villa in February, when manager Fabian Hurzeler substituted a distraught Baleba after only 22 minutes in order to save him from a second yellow card.
So which version of Baleba would United be signing? Time will tell, but there is little doubt about his ceiling. He is still only 22, still learning the game, and has already come a long way. He reflected on his time at Lille: “Defensively, tactically, I can say it: [I was] rubbish, zero.” He will only improve working with Michael Carrick.
At his best, Baleba roves from one end to the other, strong and quick, skilful and intelligent, protecting his defence not only with his defensive interventions but in his ability to escape trouble and relieve pressure. There have been some questions over his positional sense, but you don’t rack up his number of interceptions without being in the right place at the right time.
Perhaps most importantly, he could blend seamlessly with Youri Tielemans, who United bought earlier this summer from Aston Villa. Tielemans has complementary characteristics to Baleba, as a penetrative passer and a careful reader of play. One takes the temperature of a game, the other runs headfirst into the eye of the storm.
Baleba does not always look at his most comfortable receiving passes from his goalkeeper on the edge of his box – he is better facing forwards – but Tielemans will fill that role, while Kobbie Mainoo and new signing Andrey Santos are well suited to that deeper build-up position. Likewise, Tielemans cannot devour 60 yards in a few seconds with the ball at his feet, as Baleba does.
![Bruno Fernandes, left, and Youri Tielemans could soon have another midfield partner](https://static.independent.co.uk/2026/08/12/21/01KZVSM9FWEWTD2V3R2MWRVQXY.jpg)
For United’s part, it is a transfer that indicates a newfound shrewdness in the way the hierarchy operates. You can see it in the retention of Carrick’s steady presence as head coach, in the acquisition of players who already know the Premier League, in the balanced age profile of the squad. Players such as Benjamin Sesko, Mainoo, Senne Lammens and Amad Diallo – and perhaps now Baleba – could have long and successful careers at Old Trafford.
Even walking away from Baleba last summer showed a certain prudence that had deserted United for much of the past decade. Where they previously blundered around the transfer market waving big cheques in the direction of players who the whole world knew were prime targets, there is a subtlety and pragmatism to the way United have gone about their business.
Now they are set to sign a player with unbridled potential, even if it may need carefully unlocking after a difficult season. Perhaps most encouragingly for United’s supporters, Baleba is not just a player they want, but exactly the profile the team needs.
summary: Manchester United are targeting Brighton midfielder Carlos Baleba, a player with immense physical and technical potential whose role remains somewhat versatile and still developing. While his valuation caused a standoff last summer, his blend of ball-recovery skills, progressive carrying, and high ceiling make him an ideal profile for United's needs. His skill set could also complement new signing Youri Tielemans effectively in the club's evolving midfield.
key_points: Carlos Baleba combines high-level defensive interventions, such as recoveries and interceptions, with elite progressive ball-carrying ability.
Manchester United considered signing Baleba previously, but valuation gaps prevented a deal when Brighton sought a fee upwards of £100m.
Baleba's form dipped during a challenging recent season marked by injuries, transfer speculation, and international duty, but his high ceiling remains evident.
His attributes are viewed as a strong stylistic complement to fellow midfielder Youri Tielemans.

title: Verstappen signs surprise new Red Bull deal
author: Jack Cozens
content:
Max Verstappen has extended his contract Red Bull Racing and will remain at the Formula 1 team until the end of the 2030 season.
The four-time champion and his future with the team has been the subject of speculation for much of the past season and a half, most prominently amid interest from Mercedes about securing his services - which were headed off last year by performance-related clauses in his contract - and this year in the wake of Verstappen's reaction to the new F1 ruleset.
The fabric of the team that Verstappen has been with for the past decade has also changed significantly in recent years, with key figures such as Helmut Marko - who was pivotal in making Verstappen a Red Bull junior before his graduation to F1 - Adrian Newey and Christian Horner all gone.
His race engineer Gianpiero Lambiase has also agreed to join McLaren "no later than 2028".
But Verstappen has now been announced at staying with Red Bull for the next four seasons, on the eve of his home Dutch Grand Prix - the last planned edition of the race at this time.
His current contract, announced in 2022, ran until 2028 with those aforementioned performance-related clauses, so this new arrangement essentially represents a two-year extension to that.
Red Bull said it was "immensely proud" to announce Verstappen's extended stay, calling it "one of the most successful and defining partnerships in F1 history".
It also called him a "defining part" of the team's "history, identity and success".
Verstappen was quoted as saying he was "really pleased with the contract extension" and thanked Red Bull itself, the racing team and team principal Laurent Mekies - who succeeded Horner last July - "for the trust they put in me".
He said he was "excited to keep working together with everyone to get back to the top again", amid a mixed start to the new rules era by Red Bull - a team he described as "like a second family for me" where "I feel very at home"
"Getting to work with Laurent now for over a year has also been great, I see a clear vision he has for the team," Verstappen added. "Everyone in Milton Keynes believes in what we are building and I am looking forward to the next chapter, fighting for more victories and competing for championships as we continue to shape the future of this team.
"To make this announcement during the last Grand Prix at Zandvoort is a great moment for me as well. Hopefully we can give the fans a special send-off for the final race."
Mekies said retaining Verstappen was "fantastic news for everyone at Red Bull, Oracle Red Bull Racing, as well as F1 and motorsport as a whole".
"His impact on our team and on Red Bull’s motorsport story has been transformational, and he has been fundamental to everything we have accomplished together," Mekies added.
"The decision to continue our journey together is rooted in the trust Max and the team have built over many years, as well as Max’s confidence in our people, our culture and our vision for the future."
summary: Formula 1 four-time champion Max Verstappen has signed a contract extension with Red Bull Racing through the 2030 season. The two-year extension follows previous speculation regarding his future and changes within the team's leadership and engineering staff. The announcement was made ahead of the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort.
key_points: Max Verstappen extended his Red Bull contract until the end of the 2030 season.
The new agreement effectively adds two years to his previous deal, which ran until 2028.
The announcement was made on the eve of the Dutch Grand Prix at Zandvoort.
Team changes during his tenure include the departures of key figures such as Christian Horner, Helmut Marko, and Adrian Newey.

title: Premier League predictions 2026-27: BBC Sport pundits pick their top four
author: Chris Bevan
content:
![MOTD, Final Score & 5 Live](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/3840/cpsprodpb/2095/live/9273cd90-998c-11f1-a7ab-8b30adf0800a.jpg)
- Published
Arsenal ended a 22-year wait to be Premier League champions last season, but can they successfully defend their crown?
That is the next target for Gunners boss Mikel Arteta, whose side finished seven points clear of nearest rivals Manchester City last time out.
So, who will challenge them in 2026-27? We asked 26 BBC TV and radio pundits to pick their top four, with explanations for their selections.
We've also asked AI's opinion, and included what Opta's 'supercomputer' came up with too.
The AI prediction was generated using Microsoft Copilot Chat - we simply asked the tool to "predict the Premier League table for the 2026-27 season".
Opta's 'supercomputer' is actually a complex algorithm that uses a model based on betting market odds and the sports analytics company's own 'power rankings', which are calculated using past results.
It has simulated the outcome of all 380 Premier League games 10,000 times and came to the same conclusion as AI, and three of the pundits.
Disagree with our expert humans or think you know more than any machine? You can make your own top-four prediction, and forecast the rest of the Premier League table, at the bottom of this page.
These predictions were made on the basis of how each squad shaped up on Thursday, 20 August, with 13 days to go until the transfer window shuts at 23:00 BST on Tuesday, 1 September.
Last season, only four teams featured in the forecasted top-four positions, but this time there are seven named, in 15 different combinations.
Overall expected ranking, using all 28 predictions is:
- Arsenal (109 points)
- Manchester City (73)
- Liverpool (38)
- Chelsea (35)
- Manchester United (21)
- Aston Villa and Tottenham (both two)
Calculated using a system of four points for a first place, three points for second, two points for third and one point for fourth.
Arsenal - 'Arteta's army marches on'
Arsenal fans in dreamland as club win Premier League title
Last year, only 17% of BBC predictors (6/35) thought they would be champions. This year, 89% (25/28) think they will successfully defend their crown and no-one thinks they will finish lower than second.
Theo Walcott: They have got the biggest advantage of all - continuity. Mikel Arteta is still there, they are coming off an 85-point title-winning season and they have strengthened rather than rebuilt.
The Bruno Guimaraes signing is massive, to add to a midfield that already boasts Declan Rice and Martin Zubimendi. Their defence was also ridiculously good last season, although William Saliba's progress after his World Cup injury is something to watch closely.
Thomas Hitzlsperger: Arsenal are the team to beat. Unlike a lot of their rivals, they kept their manager and, every season, the team plays together and gets additions.
I still don't expect Arsenal to play nice football in the sense that I am excited to watch them play. I just think they really know what it takes to win, and they are going to do the same again this season.
Danny Murphy: It is always hard to call it now, especially when it feels like all the top teams have a lot of business to do before the transfer window shuts, but I can't look past Arsenal as champions.
The main reasons being the momentum and confidence they will have from winning the Premier League already, but also the consistency of having the same manager and same players and just sprinkling even more quality on top.
They have not lost any of their best players and they have got a group who know what the manager expects from them and are completely on board with it. Arteta didn't need to spend half the pre-season drilling them with his methods like a new manager has to.
Joe Hart: It's really important how Arsenal handle the scrutiny of being champions, but they will totally understand that and what is coming their way.
Leon Osman: They look like a team that are ready to have a run at winning three titles in the next four or five years.
Teams like United in the early Premier League days, Arsenal under Arsene Wenger and Jose Mourinho's Chelsea give me the vibes this team does. And the way they've strengthened brilliantly states the league isn't their only objective this season.
Matt Upson: They are my favourites again but I don't see them running away with it. Staying at the top is always harder - ask any manager - and you also have to remember there were spells when they looked like they had run out of steam last season and were grinding out results a lot of the time.
The biggest challenge for Arteta this year will be picking the right team, or rather resting the right players, for the right games and keeping players engaged and ready to step in when needed.
Chris Sutton: He will have to try to keep everyone happy but if you are fighting on all fronts, that's possible. They do look like they are at a different level, squad-wise.
They won the title in a bit of a different way so it will be interesting to see how they go about it this time, but it does look on the face of it like they can beat you up, or just play through you.
Arteta delighted with trophy while Maresca is 'concerned'
Nedum Onuoha: Watching them against City [in the Community Shield], you knew how they were going to play and so did their players. Arsenal have not just spent pre-season getting ready for this, they have spent the past five or six years building.
Glenn Murray: They have had continuity for several seasons now, plus winning the league has given the group a wave of belief that will see them win another title.
Michael Brown: It's theirs to lose. Arsenal should win the league because of the transition at other clubs, but also because of the quality and rhythm they have already got.
Rachel Brown-Finnis: Great squad depth and additions this summer. Arteta's army marches on!
Troy Deeney: They are the best team and they going to win the league by a comfortable margin. My only question is can they win the Champions League too? I still think they need an extra player in on that left-hand side to get that done.
Sue Smith: The way Bruno played in the Community Shield, it felt like he's fitted in already. There are probably still players that they will look to bring in, but they have got a couple of great options in every position now.
Ellen White: Bruno gives them something different again because he is so tenacious, an absolute warrior. Their midfield is formidable now, with Rice, Bruno, and Martin Odegaard to go in there, and then you have got Miles Lewis-Skelly too, almost saying "I'm still here" after the talk of him leaving. It's a great problem for Arteta to have.
I don't know if they will get another number nine this summer or not, but I still think they have more potential to be champions than any other team.
Tony Pulis: They are already strong enough defensively and they can score goals from everywhere. If they get the centre-forward they are looking for, they are going to be better than they were last year.
Shay Given: They might miss out on the title unless they sign a top striker in the next couple of weeks to help with the goal situation.
Paul Robinson: If Victor Osimhen comes in from Galatasaray, and they get Villa defender Ezri Konsa too, then it's a different conversation. But they are not the only team still trying to get deals done.
Man City - 'They are rebuilding but will still be up there'
'He's the professor' - Rodri's Manchester City journey
City were the BBC predictors' pre-season favourites in eight out of their 10 seasons under Pep Guardiola from 2016 onwards, and were champions six times during that period. But before their first campaign with Enzo Maresca in charge, only 12% (3/26) think they will reclaim the title.
Thomas Hitzlsperger: City are the only English club to have been ever-present in the Champions League since 2011, which is an achievement in itself when you think about how competitive the top of the Premier League is.
With Pep Guardiola, I would always say they would finish in the top four, but now he has gone, and it is always so tough to follow someone like that. Maybe this is the year that City finally drop out.
Shay Given: I don't think Pep leaving means we will see what happened when Sir Alex Ferguson left United. Instead, I am expecting the opposite, because of a fresh voice in the dressing room. These players have not won the Premier League in two years so they will be hungry for success. City will be number one.
Troy Deeney: My prediction for City is not based off what happened in the Community Shield, it is based off what I saw with Enzo Maresca at Leicester and Chelsea.
I am not sure he has got that ability to really demand what he wants. Pep has taught all these coaches, but only Arteta has tweaked it and kind of said "I am going to use all the principles, but this is my way of doing it".
I don't want to be disrespectful, but Maresca is a BTEC version of Pep Guardiola. He plays a certain way and has no other way of dealing with it. You saw on Sunday how bad City were defensively but all of his teams are wide open, and he is still doing that now, even with better players - top-class players.
Joe Hart: City were clunky against Arsenal in Cardiff but I don't think they will over-react to one poor game. I think they still believe they've got the team and the quality to challenge.
Theo Walcott: Maresca replacing Pep is obviously a gigantic question mark, but City's squad is still absurd. The problem is the transition from Pep to Maresca, plus losing Rodri and others.
Nedum Onuoha: City have still got a bunch of players who have won the title before, but they have got a new manager and have also lost some of their more senior players.
Anita Asante: Maresca's playing style is not that dissimilar to Pep's so there is not this massive change in terms of the team's identity. They have still got some fantastic forward players too, but Rodri leaving is massive because we know how pivotal he has been at the club.
It's the same with losing John Stones and Bernardo Silva too. They were leaders in the dressing room and they will be missed there, as well as on the pitch.
Leon Osman: That signals problems for me, even with Erling Haaland there.
Pat Nevin: Midfield, management, you name it - City are rebuilding. I will be surprised if they win it, but they will still be up there.
Rachel Brown-Finnis: They still have some big guns, but will be too inconsistent to win the league.
I'm leaving with an incredible sense of peace - Guardiola
Matt Upson: Even if Maresca struggles a bit at first, you look at the quality and experience in their squad and the goals in their team, and they still have enough to stay up there. I can't leave them out. City had that huge drop-off under Pep in the season before last, when they were terrible for a few months, and they still made the top four.
Danny Murphy: I look at the firepower City have got and, whoever the manager is and whoever they are playing against, they are still going to be able to score a lot of goals and win a lot of games. I would still have them as being Arsenal's nearest rivals.
Chris Waddle: The City midfield of Kevin de Bruyne, Rodri, Bernardo Silva and Ilkay Gundogan that won so much has all gone now, and they are replacing them with people where the expectation is they will grow into that City shirt.
They are trying to build a new team, and it might take them a year or two. They will still be in the top four, but the question is how well - and how quickly - they gel together.
Steph Houghton: Arsenal will be tough to beat but I still think City will push them, as soon as their players get back into a bit of form and find some rhythm.
This is the next era for City, with a new manager and new players, and I think the likes of Elliot Anderson will come good. Then there is Jeremy Doku and Rayan Cherki, plus Haaland of course. It's still a world-class squad.
Sue Smith: They are going to add to their midfield so it's hard to predict what they will do until the end of the transfer window and we know who they've got, but Anderson will be a success there.
There is a lot of pressure and expectation on his shoulders but he is a brilliant player and it just seems like he'll be able to cope with that.
Ellen White: City want Enzo Fernandez from Chelsea, but I am not sure he is the right player for them. And, whoever comes in, it is going to take time to find the right balance in midfield.
Chris Sutton: There's no doubt the pressure will be on Maresca from the off, and replacing Rodri is nigh on impossible. They are in for Lille's Ayyoub Bouaddi, who is a talented player but he is 18, and would be a massive gamble.
Michael Brown: City are in transition, and a lot depends on who they bring in. But if they have a really impressive end to the window, it changes everything.
Liverpool - 'A work in progress but Iraola is exciting'
![Graphic showing last season's Premier League top six](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/2d6b/live/96f5fd60-9b18-11f1-b8e1-e7ef86eff0e6.png)
New Liverpool manager Andoni Iraola's Bournemouth side finished one place and three points behind the Reds last season
Last season, 22 of 35 BBC predictors had them down as champions and only three thought they would finish lower than second. This time, only four of 28 have them finishing higher than third.
Danny Murphy: Liverpool might need a bit more time before they are challenging for the title again. I am also not sure whether they think they have already got enough to replace Mohamed Salah by bringing in Victor Munoz and maybe giving Rio Ngumoha a bigger role, or whether they are really going to go for Paris St-Germain's Bradley Barcola, or someone like him, in the next few days.
Michael Brown: They look light to me as I write this. Who are they going to get to improve them?
Lindsay Johnson: Liverpool and Chelsea are in the same boat because both new managers will take time to settle in, and Liverpool probably don't have a big enough squad to last a full season playing the football Andoni Iraola plays.
Theo Walcott: Liverpool are probably the hardest team to call. Iraola is an excellent manager and if Alexander Isak and Florian Wirtz have big seasons, they could absolutely push Arsenal for the title.
Thomas Hitzlsperger: I've gone for them to finish second because I really like the way Iraola's teams play. Also, I am kind of biased here because I am really hoping Wirtz has the season now that people expected him to have last year.
Paul Robinson: Wirtz looked a different player towards the end of last season and they also have a manager who has proved himself, and is Premier League ready.
Sue Smith: I know it's a completely different level and expectation managing Liverpool and it's going be interesting to see how he does in that sort of step up, but all you can judge Iraola on is what he's done at Bournemouth and I think he's been brilliant. Defensively is my concern, though. Especially the right-hand side.
Anita Asante: It will take time for Liverpool to adapt to Iraola's style, which is closer to Jurgen Klopp's. I am excited, because that means high-tempo, high pressing and playing on the front foot, but that's why it's even more important they sign reinforcements to strengthen their defence.
Glenn Murray: They have got all the forward players you could dream of, but Iraola has a big headache when it comes to finding the right balance between attack and defence.
Troy Deeney: They are decently balanced although I still think they need an additional left-back and an extra midfielder. Ultimately they have got one X-factor - Isak. He is a top goalscorer who has got a point to prove because everyone has written him off.
Rachel Brown-Finnis: Iraola is Liverpool's most exciting signing in recent years. Liverpool's football DNA will be back.
Leon Osman: Liverpool are a work in progress. Older players leaving, new managers in. Some good signings at the back but will Iraola get them firing straight away? I'm not sure.
Chelsea - 'They are potentially going to be unplayable'
Chelsea sign Welbeck - watch all of his Premier League goals from last season
Last season, Chelsea figured in all 35 top-four predictions, and finished 10th. This time, they are in 21/28 predictions, with five people backing them to be runners-up.
Pat Nevin: As usual my top four is only a guess but it's the triumvirate of Joao Pedro, Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers up front that makes me back Chelsea to be in there more than anything else. They are a group who are exciting, and brilliant as well. It will be fascinating to see how they get on.
Sue Smith: They have been using Palmer and Rogers as two number 10s in pre-season, which is frightening. They are potentially going to be unplayable.
Michael Brown: They have got all this talent but as usual it is still about them finding the right balance. They might surprise people and be solid.
Joe Hart: Their squad is well built, and they don't have European football.
Nedum Onuoha: It's a ridiculous anomaly for teams like Chelsea or Spurs to not be in Europe, and being able to focus on domestic football while they have both been spending such big money.
Matt Upson: There seems to have been a big change in their transfer policy and the balance of their squad looks a lot better for them to be able to win trophies.
Troy Deeney: No Europe means more time on the training pitch, so Xabi Alonso will be in a great position to figure out what works best. I wouldn't be surprised if they finished second, because I can't split them, City or Liverpool.
Glenn Murray: Alonso is coming in with a point to prove after what happened at Real Madrid, and he has made some shrewd signings, including some experienced players who can help their young team-mates harness their enormous potential.
Chris Waddle: Having Danny Welbeck and Jordan Henderson in the team will be like having a coach on the pitch. Yes they are 35 and 36 now, but I played in the Premier League until I was 36 and I didn't really find it hard. You still have your brain and, even if your legs have gone a bit, you can have legs around you.
Steph Houghton: That experience is what people were saying they were missing last season.
Tony Pulis: I really rate Alonso and bringing in Welbeck and Henderson was almost an act of genius because if, you look from the outside, the problems at that club are because there has been no-one in the dressing room to pull up the young players when that has been needed.
Thomas Hitzlsperger: Chelsea are probably the team I am most optimistic about when I look at the manager.
Anita Asante: Alonso will give them structure and bring an identity to the team but he won't restrict the players. I feel like he will give them the freedom to express themselves.
Theo Walcott: Alonso gives them the stability they have been missing. If Palmer stays fit, I can see them being one of the most consistent teams outside the title race.
Man Utd - 'The mood at the club feels different'
Carrick is pushing to improve the squad this summer
Last season, none of the BBC predictors backed United to make the top four, and they finished third. This time they figure in 14/28 predictions, although only one of them has them improving on last year's position.
Thomas Hitzlsperger: United can stabilise themselves this season.
Michael Brown: The legs of the squad is still a concern, and the Champions League could make them unstable.
Anita Asante: The mood at the club just feels different, compared to how dysfunctional they were under Ruben Amorim or Erik ten Hag.
Ellen White: Unlike last season, Carrick has got Champions League football to contend with. I like Youri Tielemans as a signing, but they need more in... and is Marcus Rashford staying?
Paul Robinson: The best thing Carrick can do with Rashford is put his arm around him and try to get the best out of him. It's difficult enough anyway to find another player at his level, but especially when you have already got him and don't have to pay anything for him.
Steph Houghton: Rashford staying would be a massive bonus because we know his quality and he has a different skillset to a lot of the forwards they have already.
Chris Waddle: They have Rashford back at the moment but is his heart in it? Or his head? I think he's had a taste of being abroad and I'd be surprised if he doesn't want to try it again.
Matthew Upson: In the time Carrick was there, from January onwards, United showed they are definitely top-four material, and they are the ones I found it hardest to leave out.
![Graphic showing how Manchester United topped the Premier League table for games played after Michael Carrick took charge in January](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1104/cpsprodpb/a165/live/2830e750-9b18-11f1-b8e1-e7ef86eff0e6.png)
Manchester United topped the Premier League table over games played after Michael Carrick took charge at Old Trafford in January
Tony Pulis: I still don't think United, over a season, will do it with what they have got at the moment. They might still get three or four in, and that changes the picture but, right now, they are short. Arsenal and City are miles ahead of them.
Troy Deeney: I've got United down as fifth. A solid year, but nothing special. I don't think they have got a great squad so they will be out of the Champions League by February and then they can concentrate on the league.
Lindsay Johnson: United's defence needs work but they may sneak in fourth.
Anyone else? - 'Villa are so good under Emery' and 'can you ever trust Spurs?'
Outstanding week and season - Emery
Lindsay Johnson: I've put Villa in there again because of Unai Emery and his experience.
Leon Osman: Villa have been brilliant the past few seasons but they keep letting their best players go. How long can Emery keep over-performing with what he's given?
Thomas Hitzlsperger: Villa being in the Champions League means they are probably going to be in the top six rather than the top four, but they are just so good under Emery.
Glenn Murray: Tottenham are going to be much better than last season. They have made some great signings and James Maddison is back fit. My only worry for them is that they still need a goalscorer.
Leon Osman: Their signings, plus injury returns should see Tottenham competing where they expect to - but can you ever trust Spurs?
Paul Robinson: Spurs had a shocker last season but this time they are on the fringes of the Champions League places, without a doubt. When Roberto de Zerbi took over last season, he wanted guarantees in the transfer market this summer - and judging by the players he has brought in, he got them.
Newcastle are miles off it, though. I cover the Saudi Pro League and Matthias Jaissle is a good coach who plays attractive football - but he needs the players and at the moment they don't have them.
Troy Deeney: After finishing 17th two seasons in a row, expecting Spurs to be in the top five is a big ask. It is Nottingham Forest who are my surprise package this year - I know people will say they have lost Anderson but, the way they play, I don't think he is a massive loss. The owner is ambitious and so is Oliver Glasner, so it is a marriage made in heaven.
Nedum Onuoha: I am going with Leeds and Sunderland to surprise people. A few people are expecting Sunderland to struggle because they are in Europe but the owners are a bit more ambitious than people realise. They won't necessarily be fifth in November, but I don't think they will be down the bottom either.
The same for Leeds. Staying up last year was huge, and now they are thinking about part two of who they want to be, and part two features things like signing a goalkeeper for Â£40m.
Steph Houghton: Sunderland are playing more games this season and have not been able to boost their squad yet, but hopefully that will happen next week. But they were seventh last time and will be there or thereabouts again, especially if they can sustain their home form.
Tony Pulis: I don't see Villa making it although they are a good side. I don't think any of the teams like Bournemouth, Brighton and Brentford - who were all in the top 10 last season - will be anywhere near the relegation places, but it is very difficult for them to get into the top four.
Danny Murphy: I am not talking about the top four, but Ipswich might surprise a few people and, out of the the ones who have come up, be the team who don't struggle.
They have spent quite a lot, and brought in about a dozen players, like Sunderland did last year, and again they have brought in a similar type of player too, with a lot of athleticism.
Their manager Gary O'Neil did all right at Wolves and Bournemouth and he will be as well-equipped as ever to know which games to go after, and when to dig in.
summary: Following Arsenal's Premier League title victory last season, BBC Sport pundits, AI, and Opta's supercomputer have shared their top-four predictions for the 2026-27 campaign. Arsenal are heavily favored by experts to successfully defend their crown due to squad continuity and strong additions like Bruno Guimaraes under manager Mikel Arteta. Meanwhile, Manchester City enters a transitional phase following Pep Guardiola's departure and the arrival of new manager Enzo Maresca, though experts still expect them to remain near the top.
key_points: Arsenal finished seven points clear of Manchester City to win the previous Premier League title after a 22-year wait.
Eighty-nine percent of BBC predictors expect Arsenal to successfully defend their championship in the 2026-27 season.
Manchester City is undergoing a rebuilding period following the exit of Pep Guardiola and several key players, with Enzo Maresca taking over as manager.
AI and Opta's supercomputer predictions align with the consensus that Arsenal and Manchester City will occupy the top two positions.

title: England vs Pakistan live: Score and latest updates from day two of the first Test
author: Kieran Crichard; Rob Bagchi; Scyld Berry; Will Macpherson; Tim Wigmore; Nick Hoult
content:
![Joe Root](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/cricket/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498938169_17872342019370_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqhaQcnQgX1lblZ3yiN-_RsPmJDQle8zhAnRj3nA8oxTY.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Joe Root](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/cricket/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498938169_17872342019370_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqhaQcnQgX1lblZ3yiN-_RsPmJDQle8zhAnRj3nA8oxTY.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
OVER 32: ENG 139/2 (Cox 41 Root 44)
Abbas starts down the hill with a maiden to Cox which will look better in the scorebook than it did in actuality. His line was all over the shop and Cox left or defended with ease.
Pakistan are so lucky that they do not have to spend a whole day in the field with a threadbare attack. Sajid Khan, their moustachioed offspinner, has to come into the side for the second Test to give it some ooomph in the field, some animation, even though Lord’s is not a spinning ground. But why not aim for spinning pitches at HQ and make it the ground’s USP?
To read Scyld’s view on the Lord’s pitch, click here.
OVER 31: ENG 139/2 (Cox 41 Root 44)
Mohammad Ali replaces Abbas and runs in up the hill as if he’s towing a caravan. Starts with a welcoming half-volley and Root flicks it through square leg for two. He hoops the next three outside off and Root is not tempted to chase them then defends the next two. Abbas is only changing ends. He bowed 10 overs off the reel yesterday from the Football Stand End but will now have a go from the Kirkstall Lane End.
![Cox drives uppishly](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/cricket/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498939725_17872353659780_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqW5LAbqXSQw_G1yEaLnMlB15NUcTKNHKqy85KLqtvPLE.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
OVER 30: ENG 137/2 (Cox 41 Root 42)
After a good start in his opening two overs, Khurram takes the silver cloche off a pie, spraying a half-volley on to Cox’s pads and he greedily clips it fine of long leg for four. After a second no-ball as the runaway train came down the track, he gives Cox some width outside off and the batsman goes for it, spooning a drive through cover point with the outside third of the bat. Two balls later he goes a touch shorter and Cox is surprised by the bounce but manages, not intentionally, to squirt it off the splice down through gully for four.
And then Khurram deals up another half-volley and Cox whosks it slickly through midwicket for four more. He’s catching up with Roo after taking 16 plus the no-ball off the over. Blogger’s curse strikes the bowler.
Jordan Cox looked excellent last night. If he can get through the much harder batting conditions today, that would be a real statement. He opened for a couple of years for Kent in the Championship, so could conceivably slot up to open when Jacob Bethell returns at three.
OVER 29: ENG 120/2 (Cox 25 Root 42)
Jordan Cox is wielding a Kookaburra bat. Can’t remember an England regular since Jos Buttler and before that Graham Thorpe who was sponsored by the Melbourne company. They don’t pick many Poms. I digress, anyway, he uses it to work Abbas of his legs for a single as England start cautiously against the moving ball in 17C temperatures and with pregnant, grey clouds above.
OVER 28: ENG 119/2 (Cox 24 Root 42)
This is a markedly better spell from Khurram than he managed yesterday. Cox leaves the big outswinger alone, chops the next down to third man for a single but the right-arm dobber beats Root a second time with the one that wobbles in and nips away and then, after a no-ball for overstepping as he got ahead of himself coming down the hill, forces Root to block in his crease.
OVER 27: ENG 117/2 (Cox 23 Root 42)
Abbas starts with the keeper back so Root walks down the pitch and clips the ball off middle through square leg for four. After one ball Rizwan comes up to the stumps. That change forces Root back to take guard on the crease line rather than 12 inches outside and he defends three and leaves one of the next four. Abbas strays on to leg stump, Root’s eyes widen but he plays it gently, slightly squared up, and doesn’t beat the infield.
![Root pushes the ball to backward point](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/cricket/2026/08/20/TELEMMGLPICT000498938169_17872341079730_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqTUEOn4-yHdlPS6WVNdiWlvmJDQle8zhAnRj3nA8oxTY.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
OVER 26: ENG 113/2 (Cox 23 Root 38)
Khurram, under oyster-shell, grey skies and the floodlights fully on, starts with a beauty, full, wobbling in to off-stump then nipping away from Root’s loose drive.
The right-armer tries to swing it the other way, spearing in the yorker but it angles too far across and Root works it to midwicket without return. A nip-backer pins him outside the line, Root defends two into the offside then pinches the strike by opening the face and running the ball behind point for a single.
Mohammad Abbas will obviously take the ball from the Football Stand End.
Hark at Will ‘Kid’ Macpherson here:
Amazing to think it is 25 years to the day that Mark Butcher made his extraordinary unbeaten 173 here against the Aussies. The first England Ashes Test victory I remember, and a formative cricketing experience for me.
summary: During day two of the first Test between England and Pakistan, England progressed to 139 for 2 after 32 overs under grey skies. Batters Jordan Cox and Joe Root continued their innings, facing bowling spells from Abbas, Mohammad Ali, and Khurram. Cox notably scored 41 runs while Root reached 44 runs.
key_points: England reached 139 for 2 after 32 overs on day two of the first Test.
Jordan Cox and Joe Root were batting on 41 and 44 runs respectively.
Bowlers including Abbas, Mohammad Ali, and Khurram shared bowling duties for Pakistan.
Play took place under grey skies and floodlights with temperatures around 17C.

title: Wright reveals Arsenal transfer worry after Lewis-Skelly exit rumours
author: Arthur Ferridge
content:
![Add Evening Standard as a preferred source](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/google_preferred_source_badge_dark.png?quality=75&auto=webp&width=960)
![Mikel Arteta calls on Arsenal to build momentum after Community Shield victory over Manchester City](https://static.standard.co.uk/2026/08/20/7/38/Ian-Wright-on-The-Overlap.png?width=1280&auto=webp&quality=75)
![Arsenal Football Newsletter](https://www.standard.co.uk/img/newsletters/newsletter_arsenal_embed_desktop.png)
Standard Sport reported last week that the player had been offered to Chelsea and Manchester United by intermediaries, casting doubt over his future with the Gunners, where he has played since he was eight years old.
No concrete interest seemed to materialise from the rumours, and Lewis-Skelly has impressed in performances against Manchester City and Como since, suggesting he is prepared to stay and fight for his place.
The emergence of those reports, though, has left Wright concerned about Arsenal’s transfer strategy. Speaking on the Stick to Football podcast, he questioned the Gunners’ approach to the market.
“I don’t know where that’s coming from because I know for a fact that’s not coming from his team,” he began. “It’s not coming from his mum. Arsenal fans need to chill out with his mum saying that she’s touting him about.
“Myles has already said he’s happy to say. Why have Arsenal not just said he’s not for sale? He’d be a great signing for Manchester United, of course he would. Look what he’s doing.
“There’s things happening and this again is what I’m worried about with Arsenal, it’s the way we’re doing business with intermediaries now. How’s that story happening when we know for a fact they’re happening and want to stay and are happy.
“Martinelli has not been contacted by anybody at the club but has been touted about everywhere. Who is doing that? Why is that happening?”
Wright went on, questioning the state of Arsenal’s finances as he pointed out the club may be pushed to sell for pure profit.
“The unfortunate thing you get when you’ve got a player who comes through the academy and breaks into the first team and does what they do, you’ve always got that noose of pure profit on them.
Read More
“When you’ve got someone like Myles who is playing well, it’s unbelievable what he’s capable of doing then of course Manchester United will see if something can happen.
“They’ve seen Guimaraes come in; they’ve seen Declan Rice. He doesn’t want to leave and that’s the thing that’s really baffling me is why Arsenal don’t just come in and say he’s not for sale.”
summary: Former Arsenal player Ian Wright has raised concerns over Arsenal's business dealings with intermediaries following rumours that young academy product Myles Lewis-Skelly was offered to rival clubs. Despite the player being happy to stay, Wright questioned why the club has not publicly declared him not for sale. He also expressed worry that the pressure for pure profit from academy players could lead to unwanted transfers.
key_points: Intermediaries reportedly offered Myles Lewis-Skelly to Chelsea and Manchester United.
Ian Wright criticized Arsenal's handling of business with intermediaries on the Stick to Football podcast.
Wright questioned why Arsenal did not simply state that the player is not for sale.
Concerns were raised about the financial pressure to sell academy graduates for pure profit.

title: Tottenham transfer news: Spurs in talks to sign Man City's Omar Marmoush and Savinho
author: Sami Mokbel
content:
![Split image showing Savinho and Omar Marmoush](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/a624/live/8092d520-9c71-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.png)
Savinho made seven Premier League starts for Man City last season while Marmoush made eight
- Published
Tottenham are in talks with Manchester City over a double deal for forwards Savinho and Omar Marmoush.
Sources have told BBC Sport that negotiations between the clubs are progressing, although an agreement has yet to be reached.
Spurs' interest in Brazilian winger Savinho dates back to 2025, when the 22-year-old opted to remain at Etihad Stadium.
But he was limited to just seven starts in the Premier League last season, and is now minded to leave the club after joining for a Â£30m fee in 2024 from French club Troyes.
Marmoush, a Â£59m signing from Eintracht Frankfurt in 2025, fell out of favour under Pep Guardiola in 2025-26 and the 27-year-old managed eight goals in 36 appearances in all competitions.
City's valuation for the pair is unclear, but the club would expect to make a significant profit on both.
Tottenham head coach Roberto de Zerbi has revamped his midfield this summer, signing Mateus Fernandes from West Ham and Sandro Tonali from Newcastle for a combined Â£185m.
But the Italian has stressed the need to strengthen his attack following the side's 17th-placed finish in the Premier League last term, scoring just 48 goals in 38 games.
Spurs remain interested in Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo, but it is unclear whether the club could finance a deal for the Netherlands international as well as moves for Marmoush and Savinho.
City have already sold a host of players this summer, including Rodri, midfielder Tijjani Reijnders and second-choice goalkeeper James Trafford.
Spurs kick off their Premier League campaign away at Brentford on Saturday (17:30 BST), while City host Bournemouth on Sunday (14:00 BST).
summary: Tottenham are in talks with Manchester City to sign forwards Savinho and Omar Marmoush as head coach Roberto de Zerbi looks to strengthen his attack. Negotiations are progressing, though an agreement has not yet been reached and Manchester City's valuation remains unclear. Spurs are also tracking Liverpool's Cody Gakpo, though potential financing for all three deals is uncertain.
key_points: Tottenham are negotiating a double deal with Manchester City for forwards Savinho and Omar Marmoush.
Savinho made seven Premier League starts last season after joining City in 2024, while Marmoush signed from Eintracht Frankfurt in 2025.
Spurs head coach Roberto de Zerbi is seeking to reinforce his attack following a 17th-placed finish last season.
Tottenham also maintain an interest in Liverpool forward Cody Gakpo.
